notes.meaning: These verses list more families of temple servants returning from Babylon. These workers did practical jobs to help the priests and Levites, such as carrying wood and water. Many of their family names sound foreign, showing that God welcomed outsiders who joined His people and served Him.

The list of temple servants continues with families like Bakbuk, Hakupha, and Harsha. Even though their work was humble and routine, God knew each family and recorded them by name. Their willingness to return showed real devotion to God's house after years in exile.

This finishes the record of the temple servant families who returned to Jerusalem. They chose to leave Babylon and help restore worship in a ruined city. God values faithful service, no matter how small the task might seem.

These verses name the descendants of King Solomon's servants. King Solomon had assigned workers to assist with building and caring for the first temple, and their families kept this role for generations. They willingly returned to serve the Lord just as their ancestors had done.

Together, the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon's servants came to 392 people. While this was a small group compared to the whole assembly, their help was vital for the daily work of God's house. Every role in God's service matters.

A group of 652 people returned from several towns in Babylon, but they could not find family records to prove they were Israelites. Lineage was important because it decided land inheritance and full inclusion in the worship community. Even without proof of their family tree, they loved God and traveled back with His people.

Three families of priests also had trouble finding their ancestral records. One family took the name of Barzillai, a famous wealthy supporter of King David, after an ancestor married one of his daughters. By preferring a nobleman's name over their priestly heritage, they lost their clear place in the family records.

These priestly families searched the public records, but their names could not be found. Because the priesthood had to follow God's law strictly, they were set aside and not allowed to serve at the altar. God's work requires careful obedience to His holy standards.

The governor ruled that these men could not eat the most holy food, which was the sacred portion set aside for priests, until God gave clear direction. A priest would need to consult the Urim and Thummim, sacred objects used to reveal God's decisions. This suspension protected the holiness of the altar while leaving open the hope that God would settle the matter.

The whole assembly returning together came to 42,360 people. When the specific family numbers listed earlier are added up, they come to a smaller number. The larger grand total likely includes people from other tribes or children who were not listed separately.

In addition to the main assembly, there were 7,337 male and female servants, along with 200 singers. Having servants and singers shows that at least some families had done well and gained wealth while living in Babylon. Their journey back to Jerusalem was marked by praise and joy.

The travelers brought thousands of animals, including horses, mules, camels, and over six thousand donkeys. These animals carried supplies, heavy baggage, and people across the long desert route. God had supplied them with the resources they needed to make the difficult journey home.

When the exiles arrived at the ruined temple site in Jerusalem, family leaders gave voluntary gifts to rebuild it on its original foundation. Even before building their own houses, they put rebuilding the place of worship first. Honoring God comes before our own comfort.

Each family gave as much as they were able, contributing large amounts of gold, silver, and garments for the priests. Darics were valuable Persian gold coins, and minas were large weights of silver. God is pleased when His people give generously according to what they have.

The priests, Levites, workers, and people then settled into their assigned towns across the land. Although their cities were still in ruins, the people were peaceful and united as one nation again. God had brought them safely back to live in the land He had promised them.
